episode_thesis: Recorded about 24 September 2026 (upload 29 Sep), with Alan Dunne guest-hosting for Niels. Nick Palus argues that markets are hard to read and predict (even the current state), so trend following should be treated as a continuous, volatility-scaled exposure that earns its place in portfolios by being short bonds in a rate sell-off (September 2026: about 80% of gains from fixed-income shorts, SG CTA/Trend about +15.25% YTD), not as something to be conditioned with VIX triggers: an Alpha Architect test finds no real edge over a static 10-month window. Dunne adds that analysts wrongly assume linear fundamentals-to-price links in complex adaptive markets. In the second half they review Andrew Ang's agentic-AI asset allocation architecture, and Palus concludes the idea has value (many portfolio methods, auditability, relaxing human bandwidth) but is undermined for research by look-ahead bias, non-reproducibility and monoculture risk, and that trend followers need no macro agent because the trend signal is itself an implicit regime indicator.

worldview_premises.premise: Even identifying the current market state is difficult, never mind predicting it; consensus forecasts are unreliable (analysts expected central-bank easing in Jan-Feb 2026, yet yields hit multi-year, in places decade, highs by September).
worldview_premises.support: Recalled quote he cannot place; the Jan-Feb 2026 versus September 2026 yield contrast.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend following's value in a multi-asset portfolio is that it deploys the opposite exposure to the core: in a rate sell-off the trend sleeve is short bonds and offsets the long bond core of a 60/40.
worldview_premises.support: September 2026 experience: rates were the strongest contributor and about 80% of the month's gains across managers came from fixed-income shorts including the 2-year.

worldview_premises.premise: Contribution to trend returns rotates across sectors over time, which is why diversification across contributors matters: rates did not trend until Q2 2026, currencies lacked trendiness, and 2022 was a rates, dollar and commodity (inflation/geopolitics) year.
worldview_premises.support: Own allocations' YTD attribution; 2026 is the third best trend year in 15 (with 2014 and 2022).

worldview_premises.premise: A smooth, low-vol yield rise earns more trend P&L than a choppy one, and when bond volatility stays contained while yields move a lot, volatility-scaled signals strengthen.
worldview_premises.support: Observed signal strength in September 2026 (correction applied to the ledger direction).

worldview_premises.premise: Triggers (e.g., VIX bands for look-back switching) are statistically fragile: they rarely activate, so a handful of episodes drives results; a continuous function has more power and is preferable.
worldview_premises.support: Alpha Architect test: high-VIX periods in the nine-year extension were only about three months; no benefit versus a 10-month static window outside 2020-2021; November 2020 vaccine month drove the apparent edge.

worldview_premises.premise: The Alpha Architect design is long-only, equal-notional, monthly rebalanced top-1 or top-2 of five ETFs (relative momentum with no volatility scaling), so it does not transfer directly to directional time-series trend following.
worldview_premises.support: Reading the note's methodology; the note itself discloses small samples.

worldview_premises.premise: Volatility belongs in trend portfolios through continuous signal scaling and risk budgeting, not through VIX switching; volatility and correlation spiking together change the capital needed for a vol target, so design should use asset volatilities and the correlation structure rather than the VIX.
worldview_premises.support: Own research philosophy ('we scale our signals by volatility'); no data quoted.

worldview_premises.premise: Timing trend following with volatility-based regime classification is very hard and unproven; in trendless periods do not over-parameterise the trend model, add complementary strategies that benefit from those regimes.
worldview_premises.support: His 'mantra' of long-term viability; he says he cannot show statistically that regime timing is worth pursuing.

worldview_premises.premise: Faster models help at turning points, but the open question is whether speed can be deployed dynamically in time to cut exposure; claims of timing indicators must be judged on false positives.
worldview_premises.support: Example: picking 3 of 33 turning points tells nothing without the false-positive count.

worldview_premises.premise: Short-lived V-shaped reversals, about one a year for four years (Liberation Day, March 2026), hurt unconstrained trend followers even though recent results were good.
worldview_premises.support: Recollection of the last four years; unclear whether linked to economic or political regime.

worldview_premises.premise: Equity breadth is deteriorating: about 45% of S&P 500 stocks have negative 3-month beta to the index (just under 20% at the dot-com peak), because AI stocks form a mini-index within a cap-weighted index; this clustering creates dispersion opportunities.
worldview_premises.support: Goldman Sachs chart (Christian Mulman, caption spelling) reported in the FT; the paper offers little explanation beyond concentration.

worldview_premises.premise: Agentic AI changes the human into supervisor and fiduciary, and the binding constraint in asset management is the finite bandwidth of human decision makers, which agents relax.
worldview_premises.support: Ang's paper (opening paragraph); CIO covering 10-15 departments, analyst covering 10-20 stocks, committees meeting monthly or quarterly.

worldview_premises.premise: Institutions value trend following because it deploys exposure faster than investment boards can decide, which is a structural advantage in inflation or shock regimes.
worldview_premises.support: A client's explanation of why they held trend in the 2022 inflation regime.

worldview_premises.premise: LLM-based research suffers from look-ahead bias (knowledge in parameters even if inputs are date-restricted), data-mining through agent votes, non-reproducibility of outputs, and monoculture risk when agents share one model.
worldview_premises.support: Disclaimers in Ang's paper plus his own elaboration; no empirical test shown.

worldview_premises.premise: A trend signal is itself an implicit regime indicator and a past-return/volatility-scaled forecast, so a trend follower needs no macro agent and its asset-class forecasts are not comparable to capital-market-assumption forecasts; only the portfolio-construction step (one or two methods today) could benefit from the multi-method agent approach.
worldview_premises.support: Mapping the Ang workflow to a trend model step by step.

decision_process.practice: Scale trend signals continuously by volatility (more volatile means weaker signal) rather than switching windows with triggers.
Volatility targeting at portfolio level uses both volatility and correlation, not the VIX; each asset has its own volatility.
decision_process.why: Correlation spikes change the dollar amount needed for a target.

decision_process.practice: Demand the false-positive count for any timing indicator before accepting it.
decision_process.why: Hitting 3 of 33 turning points is not evidence.

decision_process.practice: In trendless regimes do not add parameters to the trend model; add complementary strategies that benefit from those regimes.
When the macro regime is unclear, diversify more and rely less on return-based capital-market assumptions.
decision_process.why: Regime estimate may be wrong and loss follows.

decision_process.practice: Run about 20 portfolio-construction methods rather than one or two, using agents for scale (heuristic, return-based, risk-based, non-traditional), with an adversarial diversifier that builds the principal component of the others and takes the opposite stance.
decision_process.why: Ang design; he sees value for the portfolio-construction step of a trend portfolio.

decision_process.practice: Agent scoring: 60% peer votes, 40% historical backtest measures (Sharpe, drawdown); human sets the policy statement and receives a CIO board memo with audit trail.
Macro agent classifies regime (expansion, late cycle, recession, recovery) with a confidence measure; asset-class agents give expected return, volatility, confidence and a memo for about 18 assets.
decision_process.why: Ang's pipeline; confidence is meant to capture regime-identification risk.

decision_process.practice: Index-product design faces a higher bar for AI use than coding or backtesting platforms, though auditable natural-language debate helps.
decision_process.why: Index products must be rules-based and defensible.

speakers.evidence_style: Reads papers closely and points to design caveats (long-only, equal notional, small sample), asks for false positives, and prefers stating limits of what can be shown statistically ('I cannot prove'); leans on his managers' attribution data and client anecdotes; gives interpretations labelled as gut feeling.

disagreements.topic: Whether volatility conditioning belongs in trend following

positions.speaker: Alan Dunne
positions.position: Notes that some managers trade faster in high volatility and slower in low, and that short-term momentum is stronger when realised volatility is higher.

positions.speaker: Nick Palus
positions.position: Uses volatility only as continuous signal scaling and risk budgeting; regime timing is unproven, and deploying speed dynamically in time is the open question.

disagreements.topic: How to explain the rise in yields

positions.speaker: Alan Dunne
positions.position: Analysts disagree heatedly; he thinks the global short-end repricing implies higher expected policy rates, and that linear causal stories ignore positioning and complexity.

positions.speaker: Nick Palus
positions.position: No strong view; the episode shows how unreliable consensus forecasts are and how hard it is to read the current state.

disagreements.topic: How far agentic backtests can be trusted

positions.speaker: Nick Palus
positions.position: Look-ahead bias, in-process data mining, non-reproducibility and monoculture risk undermine representative backtests, though the architecture still has value.

positions.speaker: Alan Dunne
positions.position: Proposes restricting to older model vintages but concedes they may be too weak, so results must be taken at face value.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: The 44% equity allocation is attributed by Palus to risk-based and heuristic weighting under an unclear regime, but he says it is his gut feeling and the paper does not show what drove the CIO agent's tilt; this is an interpretation, not a finding.
Palus argues triggers lack statistical power yet reports an apparent edge for one condition that traces to a single month; he does not test continuous scaling versus triggers himself.
The Alpha Architect note is long-only relative momentum, so using it to discuss directional trend following is a category mismatch (Palus flags this himself).
Dunne's contention that analysts assume linear causality is a general complaint without examples tied to specific analysts; the short-end inference (growth or Iran) is a hypothesis.

Goldman's negative-beta chart is accompanied by little explanation in the paper; the proposed 'AI mini-index' mechanism and the dispersion/long-correlation implications are unsupported by data in the discussion.
Claim that agents use a debate/audit trail to be auditable conflicts with the stochastic nature of outputs: auditable reading of a debate does not make it reproducible.
Palus's claim that adding trend to a 60/40 helps in rate sell-offs rests on one month of data (and 2022); it does not address periods when bonds and trend lose together.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Palus gives few forward-looking inputs: he says he cannot read or predict the state of the market. Inputs he treats as informative are volatility-scaled trend signal strength (bond move larger than bond volatility), the volatility and correlation structure (for vol targeting), and the macro regime confidence (for diversification). Dunne's input is the short-end of the yield curve as a gauge of expected policy rates, and positioning/barriers/hedges as amplifiers of fundamental news. Horizons are days to months; none are explicit.
reader_inferences: (reader) Palus's stance is epistemic humility: because the current state is hard to identify, he prefers continuous, rules-based exposures and more diversification over discrete regime calls, which also explains why he is sceptical of both VIX triggers and macro agents for trend.
(reader) His trend-following defence is structural (opposite exposure to the core, speed versus slow boards), not a claim of predictive skill.
(reader) The two halves are connected by the same theme: where a process adds discretionary or parameter freedom (triggers, agent voting), statistical validation weakens.
(reader) Dunne's complex-adaptive-system framing implies that forward price effects depend on positioning, which he does not quantify here.
